The row security chapter is where the two ways around a policy are named together — the role attribute and the table owner's exemption. This package reports them as separate findings because the remediation differs: one is ALTER ROLE, the other ALTER TABLE.

SEC.PRIV.ROLE_CREATEROLE.note: The role attributes chapter documents the PostgreSQL 16 change this rule's wording depends on: a CREATEROLE role can no longer alter or grant privileges it does not itself hold, and may only administer roles it created. That is why this is reported at medium as durable access outside the deployment process, not as the blanket escalation older write-ups describe.

SEC.PRIV.ROLE_SUPERUSER.note: The role attributes chapter states that a superuser bypasses all permission checks except the right to log in. That is the basis for reporting it as making every other protection in the database advisory, and for this finding standing in for BYPASSRLS and CREATEROLE, which a superuser holds by definition.

CREATE ROLE documents SUPERUSER as an attribute set at creation and changed with ALTER ROLE — which is what makes the remediation a one-statement change once nothing depends on it, rather than a migration.

SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER.note: CREATE FUNCTION documents SECURITY DEFINER as executing with the privileges of the user that owns it. That is what makes EXECUTE on such a routine a bounded loan of the owner's rights rather than an ordinary privilege — the reason this rule reports the construction even when it is done correctly.

MySQL's stored object access control chapter documents the same DEFINER semantics for routines, which is why this rule is served on both engines. What MySQL has no equivalent of is a per-routine search path, so the escalation rule SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_MUTABLE_PATH does not apply there and is not reported.

SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_MUTABLE_PATH.note: CREATE FUNCTION's writing-security-definer-functions-safely section states the hazard directly and names the remedy: a SECURITY DEFINER function should have its search_path set with a SET clause attached to the function, because otherwise unqualified names resolve through the caller's path.

SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_MUTABLE_PATH.applies_to: PostgreSQL 18 (the advisory predates it; the mechanism is unchanged)
SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_MUTABLE_PATH.note: The project's own advisory on an uncontrolled search_path element. It is cited for the mechanism rather than for the version: a role able to create objects in a schema that comes earlier in the resolution order can have its own function called in place of the intended one, and the SET clause is what removes the caller's path from the decision.

SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_NO_PATH_IN_MIGR.note: The CREATE FUNCTION page carries an explicit writing-SECURITY-DEFINER-safely section: it states that a SECURITY DEFINER function should have its search_path set to exclude any schemas writable by untrusted users, and shows SET search_path on the function as the way to do it.
The schemas chapter documents search_path as a session setting resolved at call time, which is what makes an unqualified name inside a definer routine depend on the caller rather than on the author.

SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_UNSAFE_PATH.note: The writing-security-definer-functions-safely section does not stop at 'set a search_path'. It states which paths are safe to set: one whose schemas cannot be written to by untrusted users, with pg_temp placed last if it is included at all. That is the sentence this rule measures rather than repeats.

The schema chapter records the change that makes this rule worth having on an older database: before PostgreSQL 15 the public schema was created with CREATE granted to PUBLIC. A database that grew through those versions usually still carries that grant on 18, so a routine pinned to public is pinned to a schema anybody can write to.

SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_UNSAFE_PATH.applies_to: PostgreSQL 18 (the advisory predates it; the mechanism is unchanged)
SEC.PRIV.ROUTINE_DEFINER_UNSAFE_PATH.note: The project's own advisory on an uncontrolled search_path element. It is cited here for the half the sibling rule does not cover: the hazard is not the absence of a path but the presence of a WRITABLE schema in whatever path resolves, which a pinned path can carry just as well as an inherited one.

SEC.PRIV.RUNTIME_DDL.note: The privileges chapter documents CREATE on a schema and on a database as what allows new objects to be made there. Reading that privilege is what this rule does — it establishes that one consequence of an injection is available, not that an injection exists.

MySQL's privileges reference documents CREATE, ALTER, DROP and the routine privileges as static privileges granted per database or globally, which is the same reading on that engine and why the rule is served by both drivers.

SEC.RLS.CHECK_ALWAYS_TRUE.note: CREATE POLICY documents that WITH CHECK governs rows being ADDED, that USING governs rows being read, and — the fact the advice turns on — that when WITH CHECK is omitted the USING expression is applied to new rows as well. So dropping the clause is a genuine fix rather than a workaround.

SEC.RLS.DISABLED.note: The row security chapter establishes the default this rule reasons about: with no row-level security on a table, every role that holds SELECT reads every row. Separation then exists only as far as each query remembers to filter, and the database refuses nothing.

CREATE POLICY documents that a policy applies only once row-level security is enabled on the table, and that ENABLE without any policy denies everything. The two statements are separate for a reason, and that is why the good example carries both.

SEC.RLS.NOT_FORCED.note: The row security chapter states that a table's owner is exempt from row-level security unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set. That exemption is invisible in the policies themselves, which is why reviewing them comes back correct on a table with this defect.
ALTER TABLE documents ENABLE and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY as two independent settings. That they are independent is the reason this is a separate finding from SEC.RLS.DISABLED rather than part of it.

SEC.RLS.NO_POLICY.note: The row security chapter states that when no policy exists for a table with row-level security enabled, a default-deny policy is used and no rows are visible or modifiable. The finding is that default-deny, seen from an application that gets empty result sets with no error.

SEC.RLS.OWNER_UNRESTRICTED.note: The same owner exemption SEC.RLS.NOT_FORCED stands on, reported from the other side: the audit did not connect as the owner. The documentation makes no distinction between the two cases, so the split is this package's, and it exists because the two need different sentences to act on.

SEC.RLS.POLICY_ALWAYS_TRUE.note: CREATE POLICY documents the USING expression as the filter applied to existing rows: rows for which it returns true are visible. A constant true therefore admits every row, while the catalog still reports the table as having row-level security and a policy.
